newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Railtrack pressed to invest at first AGM.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Railtrack pressed to invest at first AGM.

text.p: Privatised British rail infrastructure group Railtrack Plc told shareholders on Wednesday that its trading in the current year to March 1997 "is broadly in line with our objectives and expectations."

In comments to the company's first annual general meeting since its 1.93 billion pound ($3.0 billion) sell off in spring this year, chairman Bob Horton said efforts to change the commercial culture of the organisation were now underway.
He said preliminary work had also begun on transforming some of its 14 major stations, including making full use of space, which will represent "a major investment programme."

However, a number of shareholders at the meeting called on the group to help plan new investments that would encourage new passenger and freight rail services in Britain, rather than working to boost earnings from its stock of real estate.
Railtrack counts many former or current rail workers and users among its shareholders and several used the meeting at London's Barbican Hall to voice concerns about future spending.
They wanted assurances that the group would try to reopen for passenger services lines closed in recent decades and also asked Railtrack to support expansion of freight opportunities.
Engineering and production director Brian Mellitt told the audience of several hundred stockholders that "investment is at levels the railway has not been assured of before".
Commercial director Michael Howell, pressed on provisions for freight, said that the firm wished to address the fact that "the vast majority of British freight traffic is going by road".
He said that it had designated 100 locations on its national network as "strategic freight sites".
These sites, mainly trackside real estate under the control of Railtrack's property management arm, could only be disposed of with the consent of major freight operators, he added.

Horton, dealing with questions on the politically-sensitive issue of the level and standard of maintenance on track, signals and other infrastructure, said investors should "be assured that finances will be there to carry out work in a timely manner".
He said his remarks applied particularly to problem areas like the approaches to London's large Euston station and its busy West Coast main line to Manchester and Glasgow.
A seven-to-eight year upgrade of this route is currently in its early stages, and is seen costing around 900 million pounds.
Within this plan, Railtrack executives told Reuters, it is looking at ways to integrate the work with possible service upgrades for passenger services and freight.
